newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: China abandons hut in disputed Spratlys-Manila.
newsitem.headline: China abandons hut in disputed Spratlys-Manila.

text.p: China has abandoned a hut-like structure in the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea near an island claimed by Manila, Philippine Defence Secretary Renato de Villa said on Saturday.

China has insisted on its right to enter the area but two days ago withdrew four armed vessels from near the two islands the Philippines is claiming, after Manila protested to Beijing it was trespassing.
"The hut-like structure is abandoned. Apparently, there is nobody there right now," he told a news conference.
De Villa said a Chinese fishing vessel remained in the area and was not a cause for concern.
The pull-out has defused recent tension in the Spratlys, a scattering of tiny islands and reefs with potentially rich oil and gas reserves.
Beijing says the entire area historically belongs to China. The islands are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
But de Villa said the Philippines would pursue its diplomatic protest as it considered the presence of the Chinese vessels an encroachment on its territory.

"The DFA (Department of Foreign Affairs) is pursuing diplomatic action in this regard and I would assume the diplomatic action will not stop at that particular situation wherein they pulled out," de Villa said.
The Philippines would continue to monitor the area around the eight Spratly islands it claims while the question of their ownership is resolved through peaceful dialogue, he said.
Earlier, the Chinese embassy in Manila said the presence of its armed naval ships in the disputed islands was normal and repeated its insistence that the islands belonged to Beijing.
"China has indisputable sovereignty over the Nansha Islands (Spratlys) and the adjacent waters," the embassy statement said.
"It is China's proper legal right and is unobjectionable that China conducted normal activities of peaceful use within the water of its own jurisdiction," it added.
Embassy spokesman Hao Yinbiao Hao said in a statement the ships were conducting only marine survey measurements in the area and had returned to China upon completion of the survey.
The two countries had a diplomatic clash over the islands two years ago and subsequently agreed not to do anything to unsettle peace in the area.
However, de Villa conceded that Philippine armed forces did not have sufficient resources to patrol the area regularly.
The issue has created an uproar in Manila, and some foreign ministry sources suggested that the military is using it to back its argument for a bigger slice of the government budget.
